section_summary: The section begins with the end of an October 1941 Radio Tokyo programme booklet, listing broadcast schedules, frequencies and languages for audiences across Asia, Europe, the Americas and the Pacific. It then contains a consular despatch about responsibility for reporting on Japanese overseas broadcasting, correspondence about monitored broadcasts, four copies of one monitoring report, and FBI translations of Japanese broadcasts from September 10–13, 1941. The broadcasts carry war news and commentary about United States policy, China, the Soviet–German war and Japan’s proposed Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere.

subfiles.title: Radio Tokyo international broadcast programme and frequencies, October 1941
subfiles.about: Lists Radio Tokyo transmission times, frequencies, languages and programme content for overseas audiences.
subfiles.summary: This continuation gives schedules for the Near East, Europe, the Americas, North America, Hawaii, Australia, New Zealand, China and the South Seas, followed by a frequency table. English, French, German, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Dutch and Malay text describes news, talks and music, and invites listeners to report reception quality. Page 365 is a heavily corrupted Thai-language page apparently belonging to the same booklet.

subfiles.title: Japanese Overseas Broadcasting
subfiles.from: S. G. Slavens, American Consulate General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Explains that the Commercial Attaché’s office has taken over reporting on Japanese overseas broadcasting.
subfiles.summary: Slavens answers the Department’s inquiry about an earlier instruction concerning proposed Japanese stations and a Far Eastern Broadcasting Association. He refers to despatch No. 173 of March 25, 1941, says the Commercial Attaché now handles the subject to avoid duplication, and forwards the latest instruction there.

subfiles.title: Advance reports of official Japanese shortwave broadcasts
subfiles.about: Offers advance copies of Japanese broadcast monitoring reports during the rapidly developing Far Eastern situation.
subfiles.summary: Free sends four advance copies of the Japanese section and offers similar expedited delivery when useful.

subfiles.title: Official Japanese Radio: North America Beam, copy 1
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japanese radio commentary on American, European, Middle Eastern and Far Eastern affairs.
subfiles.summary: The report records claims that Japan’s navy deters American war entry, that Allied positions are weak and that Japan’s Axis ties remain firm. It also covers China war propaganda, Wang Jingwei’s claimed legitimacy, an alleged United States–Chongqing mineral agreement and Japan’s response to an oil embargo.

subfiles.title: Official Japanese Radio: North America Beam, copy 2
subfiles.about: Duplicates the monitoring report on Japanese broadcasts concerning war, diplomacy and the oil embargo.
subfiles.summary: A second copy of the four-page report on American war entry, Allied strength, China, the Middle East and oil shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Official Japanese Radio: North America Beam, copy 3
subfiles.about: Duplicates the monitoring report on Japanese broadcasts concerning war, diplomacy and the oil embargo.
subfiles.summary: A third copy of the same four-page report, including commentary on United States policy, Axis ties and Chinese affairs.

subfiles.title: Official Japanese Radio: North America Beam, copy 4
subfiles.about: Duplicates the monitoring report on Japanese broadcasts concerning war, diplomacy and the oil embargo.
subfiles.summary: A fourth, less clearly reproduced copy of the report on American, European, Middle Eastern and Far Eastern subjects.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of advance broadcast reports
subfiles.about: Thanks Free for advance Japanese broadcast reports and welcomes future copies of material of special interest.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton appreciates the expedited copies and leaves the choice of future advance material to Free.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of translated Tokyo broadcasts, September 10–15, 1941
subfiles.about: Transmits translated transcripts of Tokyo radio broadcasts for September 10–15, 1941.
subfiles.summary: Hoover sends the transcripts to Berle by special messenger for information.

subfiles.title: Station JZK Program, September 10, 1941
subfiles.from: Station JZK; translated for the FBI
subfiles.about: Records Tokyo news and commentary, including a long address promoting Greater East Asian mutual prosperity.
subfiles.summary: News items range from Yoshizawa’s appointment to French Indochina and the Soviet–German war to Iran and Anglo-American affairs. A commentator favors German victory and attacks British conduct in Southwest Asia. Koji Okubo’s extended address argues that Japan’s history, geography and culture justify leadership of a Greater East Asia mutual prosperity sphere.

subfiles.title: Station JZK Program, September 11, 1941
subfiles.from: Station JZK; translated for the FBI
subfiles.about: Summarizes a poorly received broadcast about Japanese naval appointments and Yoshizawa’s mission.
subfiles.summary: The recorder notes heavy static and inaudible passages. Legible portions cover naval personnel changes, Roosevelt’s forthcoming speech and commentary on Japan’s plans in French Indochina.

subfiles.title: Station JZK Program, September 12, 1941
subfiles.from: Station JZK; translated for the FBI
subfiles.about: Reports Roosevelt’s Atlantic naval order and wide-ranging Japanese radio coverage of war developments.
subfiles.summary: The broadcast treats Roosevelt’s response to the USS Greer incident as a further step toward American war entry and relays a purported embassy explanation of “defense waters.” Other items concern Japanese mobilization, fighting in China, the European war, Iran and Manchukuo. The final page notes that domestic news recording was cut off.

subfiles.title: Station JZK Program, September 13, 1941
subfiles.from: Station JZK; translated for the FBI
subfiles.about: Records extensive criticism of Roosevelt’s naval policy and a broadcast addressed to children in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The news relays German, Italian and Japanese criticism of Roosevelt’s “shoot first” order, alongside reports on Atlantic shipping, aid to the Soviet Union, Asia and the European war. Commentary briefly addresses war preparation. A children’s segment urges patriotic service by describing Japanese schoolchildren helping shops and families affected by military service; the transcript ends with music and programme notices.
